sentences.text: Terrestrisuchus was an extinct genus of very small early crocodylomorphs measuring about 76 cm in length, though its extremely long tail added another 50 cm to its total size. This slender animal featured stylized legs and a short, shallow body.

Its back was protected by paired rows of osteoderms, which are bony plates embedded in the skin. These leaf-shaped osteoderms were longer than wide and featured a prominent front spur that slid under and interlocked with the scute in front of it.
Although Terrestrisuchus did not look like a crocodile at first glance, its skull was very similar to that of crocodiles.
The acetabulum of Terrestrisuchus is perforated, forming an opening between the hip bones, a feature linked to its rigidly sutured hip bones with an elongated, non-mobile pubis.
This creature possessed tightly packed gastralia, or belly ribs, which were part of its unique skeletal structure.
The dimensions of Terrestrisuchus's orbit and scleral ring suggest it was a cathemeral animal, active during both day and night.

The first fossils of Terrestrisuchus were discovered by Professor K. A. Kermack and Dr. Pamela Lamplugh Robinson in the spring of 1952 at the Pant-y-ffynon Quarry near Cowbridge, Glamorgan, South Wales.

Terrestrisuchus was formally described and named by P. J. Crush in 1984. The generic name emphasizes its terrestrial lifestyle, while the specific name is derived from the Latin word for its light, graceful build. The authority for the genus is attributed to Crush, 1984.

Experts believe Terrestrisuchus was likely terrestrial and fast, feeding on small prey such as insects due to its size. It had thin, serrated teeth indicating it was a carnivorous generalist pursuit hunter of small to mid-sized prey.
Abundant rhynchocephalians, including Clevosaurus cambrica, likely formed a large part of Terrestrisuchus's diet, possibly evidenced by bite marks on their bones.

The interlocking osteoderms provided rigid support for the body and limited spinal flexibility, aiding in supporting the body on land. This rigidity was complemented by rigidly sutured hip bones with an elongated, non-mobile pubis, unlike modern crocodilians.
Terrestrisuchus likely did not use the hepatic piston breathing method found in modern crocodilians.
Microstructure of Terrestrisuchus limb bones indicates a relatively fast growth rate compared to other archosauriforms and pseudosuchians.
In 1984, Crush recognized Terrestrisuchus's close relationship to the German sphenosuchian Saltoposuchus and erected the family Saltoposuchidae for both genera.
Terrestrisuchus lived during the Late Triassic in what is now Wales, United Kingdom, specifically from 237 to 227.3 million years ago during the Carnian stage.

Terrestrisuchus inhabited a chain of tropical, low-lying islands in southern Britain alongside small dinosaurs and abundant rhynchocephalians. It was a coastal species, which is unusual for basal crocodylomorphs typically found in inland floodplains. Terrestrisuchus likely inhabited forested karstic environments with fissures and sinkholes eroded into limestone.
While Crush reconstructed Terrestrisuchus as a quadruped, subsequent studies have debated whether it may have been bipedal instead.
A 2013 re-evaluation concluded that evidence supported Terrestrisuchus as a distinct genus rather than a synonym of Saltoposuchus.
